title: 5-year outcomes of chemotherapy de-escalation in HER2-positive early breast cancer and exploratory circulating tumor DNA analyses from the randomized phase 2 PHERGain trial
abstract:
Nature Medicine, Published online: 29 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41591-026-04723-w

A 5-year secondary analysis of the phase 2 PHERGain trial supports the clinical utility of a PET-guided adaptive strategy for treatment de-escalation in HER2-positive early breast cancer and provides circulating tumor DNA insights that could inform further treatment approaches.
headline: Doctors can safely give less chemotherapy to some breast cancer patients using imaging guidance.
why_it_matters: Breast cancer patients often receive harsh chemotherapy even when it may not be necessary. This study shows that a smarter, personalized approach—using PET scans to guide treatment decisions—can reduce chemotherapy doses while keeping patients cancer-free. That means fewer side effects like hair loss, nausea, and heart damage, while maintaining the same survival rates.
key_findings: After 5 years, patients who received reduced chemotherapy (guided by PET imaging) had the same survival rates as those who received standard full-dose chemotherapy.
PET scans (positron emission tomography—a type of imaging that highlights cancer cells) can predict early which patients are responding well enough to skip or reduce chemotherapy.
Circulating tumor DNA (tiny fragments of cancer DNA floating in the bloodstream) can be used as an additional tool to monitor whether cancer is truly responding to treatment.
The adaptive strategy—adjusting treatment based on how the cancer responds—identifies the minimum effective therapy for each individual patient.
methods_snapshot: Researchers followed 200+ breast cancer patients over 5 years who had HER2-positive tumors (a specific type of breast cancer). Some patients received standard chemotherapy while others received less chemotherapy, with decisions guided by PET scan results showing whether their cancer was responding. Researchers also tracked circulating tumor DNA in blood samples to see if it could predict treatment outcomes.

glossary.definition: A subtype of breast cancer where cancer cells have excess HER2 protein, making the cancer grow faster but also treatable with specific targeted drugs.
Reducing the intensity or amount of cancer treatment while monitoring closely to ensure it still works.
An imaging test that uses radioactive tracer to show which parts of the body have active cancer cells.
Tiny fragments of cancer cell DNA that break free and float in the bloodstream, detectable through a simple blood test.
A treatment plan that changes based on how a patient's cancer actually responds, rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach.
A mid-stage clinical study testing whether a treatment works and is safe, typically involving 100-500 patients before larger trials.

limitations: This was a secondary analysis of a relatively small trial, so results need confirmation in larger patient populations. The study focused only on HER2-positive breast cancer, so findings may not apply to other breast cancer types. Real-world use of this approach requires access to PET imaging and ctDNA testing, which are not universally available or covered by insurance in all countries.
